title: Instruction That Improves Itself
author: Dunce
source: AI in Education, Dunce's Substack (dunce.substack.com), September 8, 2026
summary: Writing about the Flourish school model, the author argues traditional school reform has been stuck for thirty years because teacher quality, the only real lever, requires slow, expensive coaching that evaporates whenever the teacher leaves, and proposes AI as a legitimate tier-1 instructor that can self-improve daily instead of resetting with staff turnover. The piece is explicit that motivation, not instructional quality, is software's first hurdle, and describes solving it by tying academic progress directly to the rest of the school day rather than relying on gamification alone. Its technical core is a described self-improving loop: an AI Observer digests every student session daily to diagnose where instruction breaks down, agents pick up those diagnoses and fix them within a day, and simulated student agents with varied personalities supply the statistical sample size a single small school cannot provide on its own. The author sets a specific bar for AI instruction, a 70% pass rate matching what human tutoring achieved at a prior company, and frames the daily-improvement compounding effect (half a percent per day compounding to roughly two and a half times better across a 180-day school year) as the mechanism by which a product-delivered system could eventually outperform even the best human direct-instruction teacher. The piece closes by arguing this doesn't eliminate teachers but frees them from repetitive explanation to instead build non-academic 'SuperPowers' like curiosity, agency, persuasion, and courage.
points: Diagnoses thirty years of stalled school reform as a structural problem, not a willpower problem: teacher-quality coaching is the only lever, and every gain it produces evaporates the moment that teacher leaves the school.

Treats motivation, not instructional accuracy, as software's real handicap versus a human teacher, and solves it by tying academic progress directly to unlocking the rest of the school day rather than leaning on gamification alone.

Describes a concrete self-improving pipeline (AI Observer diagnoses low-pass-rate lesson levels daily, agents A/B test fixes in the live system) that closes the loop between finding an instructional problem and fixing it within a single day rather than a semester or year.

Uses simulated student agents with varied personalities (distracted, focused, playful, anxious) to solve the small-school sample-size problem that would otherwise take years to accumulate through real students alone.

Frames a small, compounding daily improvement rate (half a percent per day) as mathematically sufficient to produce a system roughly two and a half times better over a single 180-day school year, arguing this is the mechanism that could eventually let a product outperform even excellent human direct instruction.
quotes: In traditional classrooms, the quality of the teacher determines the outcome far more than the lesson plan or the curriculum. The only real lever is training: observe a teacher, coach them, observe again. It is slow, it is expensive, and every gain evaporates the moment that teacher leaves.
a good teacher motivates students because they are right there. Software has none of that, and a product students don't want to use is worth nothing no matter how good its instruction is

If you are using whole class direct-instruction, your advanced students are bored, the instruction lands well with the middle 50% of the class, and your struggling students are confused. When you use AI for tier 1, your advanced students rocket ahead because they are no longer limited by what the rest of the class needs, your middle 50% do just fine with about the same amount of repetition as whole-class, and now your struggling students get direct support from the teacher every day.

An AI Observer that digests all sessions each day, diagnoses where instruction breaks down, and files the problems. Next. Simulated students supplying the sample size a single small school can't. Next. Agents that pick up those filings from the Observer and fix them, so a problem found Tuesday is gone Wednesday. This Fall.
After several years of refinement, 70% of those students passed the assessment we gave immediately afterward. Seventy percent is our bar for AI instruction.
Suppose the system gets half a percent better each day. Over a 180-day school year, that's roughly two and a half times better than where it started.
None of this removes the teacher. It removes the part of the job that was never a good use of a human being: delivering the same explanation to the same confusion for the thirtieth time.

Every school on earth already runs uncontrolled experiments on children. A new curriculum, a new schedule, a teacher trying something different third period, these are experiments, just unmeasured ones, and nobody calls them that. What's different here isn't that we're experimenting. It's that we're measuring, and that a change that hurts students shows up in the pass rate within a day and gets pulled.
